title: Tonguing and a stiff reed
summary: Questions on tonguing, a change of reed, and a reminder of playing with Kid Thomas on a soft reed.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Another thing about the tonguing, I wondered if you'd ever thought much about tonguing? No, I never thought. Most jazz musicians don't pay much attention. They might really have double tonguing and things at times. No, I never were. When you attack a note real sharp, do you start to say like the syllable T or two or do or what do you sort of do? How does your tongue work? Well, your tongue cut it off. Let's see, you got a read on it, Inch? Yeah, I've got lots of reads. You better put another one on and you read your thing for that.
Yes, I've got a new one here. What kind you use, an avandor? No, this is a Drico. This one here. It's only a number two as a sophomore. I'm going to wipe off the list. Yeah.
We didn't have any intention to try to get you there. No, I'll give you some idea what a... Because he's playing the Albert systems like. It wasn't the idea that we wanted to make the

award for playing. I just thought we had to plan that we wanted to refer to something like a certain key or a certain thing in a couple minutes ago last year. I'm not going to keep you wrong, but I don't think we'll actually be done. Is that a new read? Yeah, give it to you. It's pretty stiff. Well, that's the stiffest I've got. This is all right. It's not a stiff one. Remember the time you went out to play with Kid Thomas and all they had was a soft read on Edmund and the Washington's. I'm not sure. And that piano was really out of two. Oh yeah. But it still sounded wonderful to all of us in the band. They all got the biggest kick out of playing with you naturally.
